Background design values

Find nearby ambient monitors, enter their reported statistics, get a correctly-combined background design value per pollutant — and a report you can paste into a modeling protocol

What this tool does and doesn't do: EPA does not publish a live, no-login API for monitored design-value statistics, so this tool cannot fetch your three years of values automatically — you still read them off EPA's own Monitor Values Report and type them in, exactly as you would by hand. What this tool adds: it finds nearby active monitors for each pollutant from EPA's own monitor list so you're not searching blind, combines the years correctly per the form of each standard (3-year average vs. highest single year, with the ozone truncation handled correctly), and produces a citation-backed report. See for the full methodology and known limitations of the underlying EPA report.

3. Design values by pollutant

For each row: find a nearby monitor (or type in a Site ID you already know), then enter the exact statistic named — read directly off EPA's Monitor Values Report for that monitor and pollutant — for each of the three years. The design value, its combination method, and its comparison to the NAAQS threshold are computed automatically.

4. Report

All entered values, computed design values, monitor citations, and the applicable caveats, formatted for a modeling protocol.

Fill in step 3 above to build this report.

Before this goes in a permit submission

  • A design value is never compared to the NAAQS by itself: the comparison is background plus modeled source impact, combined per the form of the standard (40 CFR Part 51 Appendix W §9.2.2).
  • Confirm each monitor is regionally representative and not itself dominated by the source being permitted (Appendix W §8.3.2) — proximity alone, which is all this tool's monitor list can judge, is not representativeness.
  • Quarterly data completeness (75% per quarter, not just per year) is not checked here; a monitor can pass an annual observation count and still fail a quarter. Confirm against the AQS design value report if a value is close to the threshold.

Sources & data notes

Monitor list: EPA's own aqs_monitors.csv (pre-generated file, downloaded from aqs.epa.gov/aqsweb/airdata), filtered at build time to criteria-pollutant monitors (SO2, NO2, ozone, CO, PM10, PM2.5 FRM/FEM, PM2.5 non-FRM/FEM, Lead) with a last sample date in the last few years. Distance shown is straight-line, not upwind direction — Appendix W §8.3.2(b) recommends the monitor closest to and upwind of the project area, with preference for similar characteristics; this tool cannot judge either of those, only proximity.

Why you still type in the values: EPA's AirData Monitor Values Report and Air Quality Statistics Report are interactive web tools with no documented public API, so the three years of values for each pollutant/statistic have to be read off the report by hand, the same way you would without this tool. Column definitions at EPA's AirData reports page. A verified download's actual CSV header put geography first, not last as that page's prose implies, and several statistic columns use internal snake_case names (first_max_1hr, second_max_1hr, annual_meanC) rather than the display names EPA documents — match on meaning, not on label, if your download's column names don't match what's shown here.

How the three years combine, and why (verified against the relevant Part 50 appendix for each pollutant):

  • 3-year average — SO2 1-hour, SO2 annual (secondary), NO2 1-hour, PM2.5 annual, PM2.5 24-hour, PM10 expected exceedances, ozone 8-hour. These standards have a multi-year form written into the CFR.
  • Highest of the three years, because the CFR form itself spans 3 years — Lead only. 40 CFR 50.16(b) defines the standard as the maximum 3-month mean for a 3-year period, and Appendix R §6 states the design value is simply the highest 3-month mean in that period.
  • Highest of the three years, as a deliberate conservatism, not a CFR requirement — NO2 annual, CO 1-hour, CO 8-hour, SO2 3-hour, and the PM10 2nd-max concentration. These standards have no multi-year form (Appendix S §5.1(b) defines the NO2 annual design value as a single year); reporting the most conservative of the three years is a choice made here, not a regulation. If your reviewing authority wants the most recent year instead, use that year's value alone.

Ozone truncation: Appendix U §3(e) truncates to 3 decimal places, it does not round. Implemented with a rounding step before truncation to avoid IEEE-754 floating point edge cases (e.g. 0.050 truncating to 0.049).

What the EPA report cannot give you:

  • SO2 3-hour secondary: no 3-hour statistic exists in either AirData report. The 1971 secondary standard (0.5 ppm, 40 CFR 50.5) was not removed by the 2024 secondary SO2 rulemaking; derive this one from hourly data if your demonstration needs it.
  • Quarterly completeness: the reports give an annual observation count; Part 50 requires 75% capture in each quarter separately. A monitor can clear the annual count and still fail a quarter.
  • PM2.5 parameter 88502: only FRM data (parameter 88101) appear in the Monitor Values Report; a nearby monitor reporting under 88502 won't show up there even though it's listed separately in this tool's monitor list.
  • Preliminary current-year data: EPA states current-year data are preliminary until 1 May of the following year.
  • Data substitution and exceptional events: the Part 50 appendix data-substitution tests are not applied by the report or this tool. Including exceptional-event data is conservative for a background value; excluding it requires the concurrence process in 40 CFR 50.14 and 51.930.

Where the report and the CFR don't quite match: EPA's report defines SO2 "Annual Mean" as the mean of 1-hour values (hour-weighted); Appendix T §5.2(a) defines the annual secondary statistic as the mean of daily means (day-weighted). These agree only when every day has the same number of reported hours; treat the report value as an approximation. Lead's "Max 3-month Avg" in the report is the maximum rolling 3-month average within a calendar year; the actual NAAQS form is the maximum over the full 3-year period, and whether a window spanning a year boundary (e.g. Nov-Dec-Jan) is captured by either year's reported value is not documented by EPA.

Rounding: design values here are rounded to the same decimal precision EPA states the standard itself (e.g. 35 µg/m³ → nearest whole number, 9.0 µg/m³ → nearest tenth), using round-half-up. This matches the precision convention but is not a substitute for the specific rounding procedure in each pollutant's own appendix; confirm for values near a threshold.

Regulatory basis for using a design value as background: Appendix W §8.3.2(c): "For many cases, the best starting point would be use of the current design value for the applicable NAAQS as a uniform monitored background contribution across the project area," with exceptions listed in the same paragraph (e.g. a modifying source whose existing facility already impacts the monitor). See also EPA-454/R-24-003, Guidance on Developing Background Concentrations for Use in Modeling Demonstrations (2024).
